Name: Charity Bentley
Badge: Reading to Write: They Say / I Say
Which version of the They Say / I Say routine (with visual texts or with annotation) feels like the best fit for your students right now? Why?:

I'm not sure I can identify which version is best for my students right now, but only because I truly believe they're both good fits and easily accessible. I do feel that beginning with the visual texts might be best for my classes, because I think they're interpret the visuals as being less intimidating and more easily approachable at first. Using the visuals first should help to up their comfort levels and confidence in sharing their opinions and insights.

Describe one way you might adapt the They Say / I Say framework to align with the types of texts your students read most often (e.g., articles, visuals, multimodal texts).:

My classes are currently interacting with nonfiction texts. I think it's possible to adapt the framework so students can read passages and interact with them through the lenses of story characters or other real people (age groups, demographics, etc.). It could be a really fun project that would be helpful with understanding characterization, motives, etc.

What, if anything, do you need help thinking through as you plan for using They Say / I Say in your classroom?:

The approach seems quite straightforward and easily implemented, so I don't think help is necessary in the beginning stages. However, continued conversation or revisiting the practice might be quite beneficial. Often, I don't have real questions until I've jumped in and tried a strategy.
